145. Imagine a society that subjects people to conditions that make them 
terribly unhappy, then gives them the drugs to take away their unhappiness.
Science fiction? It is already happening to some extent in our own society.
It is well known that the rate of clinical depression had been greatly
increasing in recent decades. We believe that this is due to disruption
of the power process, as explained in paragraphs 59-76. But even if we
are wrong, the increasing rate of depression is certainly the result of
SOME conditions that exist in today's society. Instead of removing the
conditions that make people depressed, modern society gives them
antidepressant drugs. In effect, antidepressants are a means of modifying
an individual's internal state in such a way as to enable him to tolerate
social conditions that he would otherwise find intolerable. (Yes, we know
that depression is often of purely genetic origin. We are referring here
to those cases in which environment plays the predominant role.)

> both pro and con on the use of ritalin with  hyper-active children.  If so

Shoot them in?  Here's one that doesn't involve kids.  I was 34
when I tried Ritalin.

After studying a variety of materials on ADD, I came to the
conclusion that I am a classic case.  It was an easy matter to
find a shrink who would concur with my diagnosis and prescribe
the Ritalin.

It took about a week for me to find an effective dosage, which
turned out to be 2.5 milligrams three times a day.  It is
interesting to note that at the time the smallest dosage that
could be purchased was 5 mg, so I had to break the tabs in half.

The effect of that 2.5 mg dose on me was profound.  I spent a
full year on Ritalin, and made some interesting observations
during that time.  I could dedicate myself to the most petty
task with ease, and could remain attentive to the most dull and
boring material for indeterminate periods of time.
Simultaneously, I found my creativity to be nearly nill, and I
couldn't play racquetball while I was on it!

After a year on Ritalin, I found myself developing a violent
temper - something that I hadn't experienced before.  This in
itself was more than enough reason for me to end my experiment.

Overall, I found Ritalin to be an incredibly powerful drug.  The
"buzz" is distinctive and not uncomfortable, but it is
definitely a "buzz."  The main effect of the drug was to wipe
out my ability to simultaneously handle multiple stimuli, a
result that wasn't always desirable.  The irritability and
temper enhancement that developed after a while were the only
noticeable side effects.  I learned a great deal about how my own
brain works during that year.  I have no regrets, but I do not
use the drug any more and I would not permit my own children to
use it.

The best book I have read on the subject was written by Thom
Hartmann, "ADD, Another Perspective," subtitled "The Hunter In
The Farmer's World."

I would be pleased to correspond individually with anybody who
wants to learn more about my experiences.  Please contact me at
<celano@ic.net>.
